args.text: ### Project Directory Setup First up, ya make a directory to keep yer Rust code in. Rust doesn’t give a toss where yer code lives, but for the exercises and projects in this book, we reckon ya make a _projects_ directory in yer home directory and keep all yer projects in there. Open a terminal and punch in these commands to make a _projects_ directory and a directory for the “Hello, world!” project inside the _projects_ directory. For Linux, macOS, and PowerShell on Windows, punch in this: ```console $ mkdir ~/projects $ cd ~/projects $ mkdir hello_world $ cd hello_world ``` For Windows CMD, punch in this: ```cmd > mkdir "%USERPROFILE%\projects" > cd /d "%USERPROFILE%\projects" > mkdir hello_world > cd hello_world ``` ### Rust Program Basics Next, make a new source file and call it _main.rs_. Rust files always end in the _.rs_ extension. If yer usin’ more than one word in yer filename, the usual go is an underscore to split ’em up. Say, use _hello_world.rs_, not _helloworld.rs_. Now open the _main.rs_ file ya just made and punch in the code in Listing 1-1. ```rust fn main() { println!("Hello, world!"); } ``` Save the file and head back to yer terminal window in the _~/projects/hello_world_ directory. On Linux or macOS, punch in these commands to compile and run the file: ```console $ rustc main.rs $ ./main Hello, world! ``` On Windows, punch in the command `.\main` instead of `./main`: ```powershell > rustc main.rs > .\main Hello, world! ``` Whatever operating system yer on, the string `Hello, world!` should print to the terminal. If ya don’t see this output, have a squiz back at the [“Troubleshooting”][troubleshooting] part of the Installation section for ways to get a hand. If `Hello, world!` did print, good on ya! You’ve officially written a Rust program. That makes ya a Rust programmer—welcome aboard!
